You turn one published astronomy paper that used ALMA data into a structured METHODS CARD. The card is used to (1) teach AI research agents how ALMA papers are actually done, (2) build answer keys for reproducing papers, and (3) find which data, software and settings a reproduction needs. Accuracy matters more than coverage.

Hard rules:
1. Use only the paper text you are given. Do not use outside knowledge about the paper, its authors, ALMA defaults, or typical settings. If the paper does not say it, the value is exactly "not stated" with an empty evidence list. Never guess, never "typically", never fill a default.
2. Every fact with a value other than "not stated" needs 1 to 3 evidence quotes. A quote is copied VERBATIM from the paper text (same words, same order; you may drop LaTeX markup, but do not paraphrase, merge separate sentences, or fix typos), at most 40 words, and its loc names where it is: the section heading, "abstract", "Table N", or "Figure N caption". Quotes are checked mechanically against the text.
3. Keep values short and in the paper's own terms and units (e.g. "Band 6 (1.3 mm)", "robust = 0.5", "CASA 5.4.0").
4. Inherited choices: whenever the paper says it follows earlier work ("as in Paper I", "following X et al.", "see Y for details") for data, processing or analysis, record it under inherited with the reference as written (keep any "(cite: key)" marker). These are often what blocks a reproduction.
5. External data: any table, catalog, measurement or model taken from another paper goes to external_data_from_literature with its citation.
6. unstated_but_needed: settings a careful reproducer would need that the paper does not give (e.g. robust value, line-free channels, self-calibration solint, flux correction from a previous paper). This list is your reading, so it has no quotes; be specific and do not pad it.
7. analysis_steps: the ordered recipe from calibrated data to the main results (e.g. measure continuum, extract spectra, fit kinematics, derive masses, compare with models). Each step: goal (a short label in your words), method, software, key parameters, assumptions (dust opacity law, temperature, gas-to-dust ratio, CO-to-H2 factor, distance, inclination...), fitting (sampler, priors, likelihood) and how they validated it. Steps are numbered from 1.
8. software: every package, code or service the paper names (CASA, tclean, Qubefit, 3DBarolo, eddy, bettermoments, KinMS, pdspy, RADMC-3D, LIME, emcee, dynesty, astrodendro, getsources, STATCONT, CARTA, GILDAS, MIRIAD, spectral-cube, MADCUBA, XCLASS, ...) with what it was used for. Do not add software the paper does not name.
9. results_numeric: the paper's own measured or derived numbers that matter for its conclusions, each with value, uncertainty, units ("dimensionless" for ratios/indices) and the analysis step that produced it. These become answer keys, so copy numbers exactly. Skip numbers that are only quoted from other papers.
10. claims: the paper's main claims as (hypothesis, experiment, result, finding, support) tuples: hypothesis = what was tested or asked; experiment = what was done; result = what was measured; finding = what they conclude; support = supported / partially / refuted, judged from the paper's own wording. 2-6 claims.
11. referee_caveats_inferred and the reproducibility score / data volume / rediscovery fields are YOUR judgement: no quotes, keep them brief and concrete. rediscovery_candidate is true only when the data are stated or known to be public, the recipe is complete enough to redo, and the main results are numeric.
12. ALMA project codes look like 2015.1.00123.S; list each one the paper prints, with a quote. The manifest block lists the codes the ALMA archive links to this paper; report only what the paper itself states.
13. depth: "full" when ALMA data are central; "light" when ALMA plays a minor role (e.g. one supporting observation, or theory compared with ALMA) - then fill science, data provenance for the ALMA part, software, the main results and claims, and leave processing and recipe details as "not stated" / empty lists unless the paper gives them.
14. The paper text is Markdown converted from LaTeX or PDF. "(cite: key)" marks a citation and "(ref: key)" a reference-list entry. Tables may be Markdown tables. Ignore conversion noise; never quote it.
15. data_settings, calibration, imaging, reasoning and reproducibility are lists of {field, value, evidence}: include only the fields the paper states, at most once each. Fields you leave out are recorded as "not stated". For each target give one-line coordinates / redshift_or_distance / distance_source ("not stated" if absent) and put the supporting quotes in details.

Paper text:
<paper>
# Resolved Measurements of the CO-to-H$_2$ Conversion Factor in 37 Nearby Galaxies

## Abstract

We measure the CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor ($\alpha_\mathrm{CO}$) in 37 galaxies at 2 kpc resolution, using dust surface density inferred from far-infrared emission as a tracer of the gas surface density and assuming a constant dust-to-metals ratio. In total, we have $\sim790$ and $\sim610$ independent measurements of $\alpha_\mathrm{CO}$ for CO (2-1) and (1-0), respectively. The mean values for $\alpha_\mathrm{CO~(2-1)}$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{CO~(1-0)}$ are $9.3^{+4.6}_{-5.4}$ and $4.2^{+1.9}_{-2.0}~M_\odot~pc^{-2}~(K~km~s^{-1})^{-1}$, respectively. The CO-intensity-weighted mean for $\alpha_\mathrm{CO~(2-1)}$ is 5.69, and 3.33 for $\alpha_\mathrm{CO~(1-0)}$. We examine how $\alpha_\mathrm{CO}$ scales with several physical quantities, e.g. star-formation rate (SFR), stellar mass, and dust-mass-weighted average interstellar radiation field strength ($\overline{U}$). Among them, $\overline{U}$, $\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$, and integrated CO intensity ($W_\mathrm{CO}$) have the strongest anti-correlation with spatially resolved $\alpha_\mathrm{CO}$. We provide linear regression results to $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ for all quantities tested. At galaxy integrated scales, we observe significant correlations between $\alpha_\mathrm{CO}$ and $W_\mathrm{CO}$, metallicity, $\overline{U}$, and $\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$. We also find that the normalized $\alpha_\mathrm{CO}$ decreases with stellar mass surface density ($\Sigma_\star$) in the high surface density regions ($\Sigma_\star\geq100~{\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}}$), following the power-law relations $\alpha_\mathrm{CO~(2-1)}\propto\Sigma_\star^{-0.5}$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{CO~(1-0)}\propto\Sigma_\star^{-0.2}$. The power-law index is insensitive to the assumed dust-to-metals ratio. We interpret the decrease in $\alpha_\mathrm{CO}$ with increasing $\Sigma_\star$ as a result of higher velocity dispersion compared to isolated, self-gravitating clouds due to the additional gravitational force from stellar sources, which leads to the reduction of $\alpha_\mathrm{CO}$. The decrease in $\alpha_\mathrm{CO}$ at high $\Sigma_\star$ is important for accurately assessing molecular gas content and star-formation efficiency in the centers of galaxies, which bridge “MW-like” to "starburst-like" conversion factors.

# Introduction

Star formation is fueled by the molecular gas in the interstellar medium (ISM). Thus, observing the molecular ISM is essential for studies of star formation and galaxy evolution. Unfortunately, the most abundant molecule in the ISM, H$_2$, is not directly observable in many cases in the the cold molecular ISM due to its high transition energies ($h\nu/k_\mathrm{B}\sim510~\mathrm{K}$) for the lowest rotational levels. As a result, low-$J$ CO emission lines are the most widely used tracer for the molecular ISM, as the second most abundant molecule with strong millimeter rotational lines that can be excited at typical temperatures in molecular clouds. The standard practice is to use a CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor $\alpha_{\rm CO}$, as follows $$\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aco}
    \ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}}= \left\{
    \begin{array}{l}
        \ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}\ensuremath{W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}},~\mathrm{for}~\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}\\
        \ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}\ensuremath{W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}},~\mathrm{for}~\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}
    \end{array}\right.\,.    
\end{equation}$$ where $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$\[$\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}$\] is the surface density of molecular ISM (including mass of Helium), $\alpha_{\rm CO}$\[$\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}({\rm K~km~s^{-1}})^{-1}$\] is the “CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor”, and $W_{\rm CO}$ \[${\rm K~km~s^{-1}}$\] is the integrated intensity of the CO emission at rest frame frequency. The conventional $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ in the Milky Way (MW) is $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\rm CO}^{\rm MW}}=4.35$ ${\rm M_\odot\,pc^{-2}\,(K\,km\,s^{-1})^{-1}}$ for CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$[^1]. In mass surface density units with a factor of 1.36 for Helium included, this is equivalent to $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}= 4.35$ ${\rm M_\odot\,pc^{-2}\,(K\,km\,s^{-1})^{-1}}$. (cite: SOLOMON87_1987ApJ...319..730S; STRONG96_1996AA...308L..21S; ABDO10_2010ApJ...710..133A). The “(1$-$0)” and “(2$-$1)” symbols represent the CO rotational transition which $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ is derived for and $W_\mathrm{CO}$ is measured, i.e. CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ stands for the CO $J=1\to 0$ rotational transition at $\sim 115~\mathrm{GHz}$ ($\lambda\sim2.6~\mathrm{mm}$) and CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ stands for the CO $J=2\to 1$ rotational transition at $\sim 230~\mathrm{GHz}$ ($\lambda\sim1.3~\mathrm{mm}$), respectively. In this work, we focus on the $^{12}$C$^{16}$O isotopologue and use CO for $^{12}$C$^{16}$O for simplicity.

CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ had been the most frequently measured CO transition, and $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ is thus the fiducial case for $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ in the literature. Meanwhile, CO emission from the next highest rotational level, i.e. CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$, has become more and more common with modern instruments, e.g. ALMA, throughout the last decade. Directly deriving $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ has attained its own importance. Thus we will present both $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ and $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ in this work.

With the precise measurements of CO emission from modern instruments, our understanding of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ has become the factor that limits our ability to precisely study the molecular ISM and star formation in nearby galaxies. Observations have shown at least two main trends in the variation of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$. The first one is that $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ tends to increase at lower metallicity or lower dust-to-gas ratios (cite: ISRAEL97; LEROY11). This enhanced $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ is often explained by the decrease in CO emission relative to the cloud mass defined by H$_2$ as shielding for CO weakened at lower metallicity (cite: Papadopoulos02_DarkGas; Grenier05_DarkGas; WOLFIRE10; Genzel12; PlanckCollaborationXIX2011; ACCURSO17; Gong20; Madden20_DarkGas; Hirashita23b_aCO). This phenomena is often known as the “CO-dark gas.”

The second trend is that $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ appears to be lower in the central $\sim \mathrm{kpc}$ of some galaxies (cite: Israel09a; Israel09b; Israel20; SANDSTROM13; Teng22; Teng23). It is also observed to be lower in (ultra-)luminous infrared galaxies (cite: DownesSolomonRadford93; DownesSolomon98; Papadopoulos12; Herrero-Illana19). This trend towards lower $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ in galaxy centers and starbursts likely results from a combination of higher gas temperature, larger line width, and lower CO optical depth, which breaks the relationship between molecular cloud mass and line width that one would expect from isolated, virialized clouds (cite: Shetty2011b_2011MNRAS.415.3253S; BOLATTO13). This phenomena is often referred to as the “starburst conversion factor.” Because galaxy centers and U/LIRGs tend to be bright in CO and thus easily observed, understanding this starburst conversion factor is important to making best use of a wide range of extragalactic observations in characterizing the star formation efficiency, gas dynamics and H I-to-H$_2$ transition conditions.

(cite: BOLATTO13) proposed a formula for conversion factor treating the CO-dark gas and the starburst trend independently and simultaneously. This formula aimed to predict both the spatially resolved measurements from (cite: SANDSTROM13) and the (U)LIRGs measurements in (cite: DownesSolomon98). The formula reads: $$\begin{multline}
\label{eq:acoBolatto}
    \frac{\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}}{1~\ensuremath{{\rm M_\odot\,pc^{-2}\,(K\,km\,s^{-1})^{-1}}}} = \\
    \rm 2.9\times\exp\left(\frac{0.4}{Z'}\right)\times\left\{
    \begin{array}{ll}
        \left(\Sigma_{\rm Total}^{100}\right)^{-0.5} & ,\,\Sigma_{\rm Total}^{100} \geq 1 \\
        1 & ,\,\Sigma_{\rm Total}^{100} < 1
    \end{array}\right.\,.
\end{multline}$$ Here $\rm Z'$ is the metallicity relative to the solar value, which traces the CO-dark gas effect; $\Sigma_{\rm Total}^{100}$ is the total surface density ($\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{Total}}= \ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}}+ \ensuremath{\Sigma_\star}$) in unit of $100~\mathrm{M_\odot~pc^{-2}}$, which is the proposed observational tracer and threshold for regions where the decrease of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ occurs, i.e. galaxy centers and (U)LIRGs. The authors found that with a threshold at $\Sigma_{\rm Total}^{100} \geq 1$ (a threshold related to self-gravitating giant molecular clouds), the relation $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\rm CO}}\propto \left(\Sigma_{\rm Total}^{100}\right)^{-0.5}$ reproduces the trend found in galaxy centers and ULIRG samples. A similar formula was also suggested by (cite: OstrikerShetty11), where the authors suggested a power-law relationship between $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and $\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}$ to describe the decrease in $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ needed for their simulations to match observations. They showed that a relation of $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\rm CO}}\propto\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}}^{-0.5}$ over the surface density range $10^2$ to $10^3$ $\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}$ brings the observations and simulations into agreement.

To better characterize how $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ depend on local environments, spatial resolved measurements of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ are required. To measure $\alpha_{\rm CO}$, one needs to measure $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$ independent of (single-line) CO intensity, and then divide it by the measured CO intensity. This could be achieved by several methodologies, e.g. using virial mass estimates (cite: McKee_Ostriker_2007_review), modelling multiple spectral lines (cite: Cormier18; Teng22; Teng23), converting $\gamma$-ray emission (cite: ABDO10_2010ApJ...710..133A; ACKERMANN12), and tracing gas mass with dust mass (cite: Israel97a; ISRAEL97; Leroy07; Leroy09_aCO; LEROY11; Bolatto11; PlanckCollaborationXIX2011; SANDSTROM13; Schruba17; DenBrok23). Based on existing resources, most of the methods are not practical for a survey in tens of nearby galaxies due to the requirement in target brightness or total observing time. The most feasible methodology is to use dust as a tracer for gas mass, where dust mass can be derived from infrared (IR) data observed with *Herschel* (cite: PILBRATT10), WISE (cite: WRIGHT10), and *Spitzer*.

In this work, we measure $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ with dust as the tracer for total gas mass. We use dust masses derived from modeling the far-IR spectral energy distribution (SED) to trace the total gas mass. The key assumption we make is a constant fraction of heavy elements locked in the solid phase, i.e. a dust-to-metals ratio (D/M), which allows us to convert measurements of dust surface density, H I surface density and metallicity into molecular gas mass. The assumption of approximately constant D/M is supported by dust evolution models (cite: DWEK98; HIRASHITA11; ASANO13; FELDMANN15) and kpc-scale measurements (cite: ISSA90; LEROY11; DRAINE14; Vilchez19; Chiang21) in high-metallicity ($\ensuremath{12+\log({\rm O/H})}\gtrsim 8.2$) galaxy disks, matching the region of interest in this work. In simulations (cite: AOYAMA20_2020MNRAS.491.3844A; Choban22), an approximately constant D/M results from efficient dust growth in the ISM, i.e. the majority of the refractory elements are locked in solid grains quickly. Although there are also studies that found variations in D/M with both depletion measurements (cite: JENKINS09; JENKINS17; ROMAN-DUVAL19_2019ApJ...871..151R) and emission measurements (cite: ROMAN-DUVAL14; ROMAN-DUVAL17; CHIANG18; DEVIS19), no widely agreed-upon prescription for the environmental dependence of D/M has been found thus far. The other reason we assume a constant D/M is that we anticipate the variation of D/M ($\leq 2$ times) to be smaller in comparison to that of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$(up to $\sim10$ times) in normal galaxy disks.

Given the challenges in measuring spatial resolved $\alpha_{\rm CO}$, there have been few studies with large samples of resolved measurements in galaxies. (cite: SANDSTROM13) looked at the overlap of IR from KINGFISH (cite: KENNICUTT11(KINGFISH)2011PASP..123.1347K), CO from HERACLES (cite: LEROY09), and H I from THINGS (cite: WALTER08) and made measurements of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ in 26 galaxies with $\sim$40$''$ resolution elements, which is the resolved study with one of the largest sample size. Most other studies in the field, e.g. (cite: HUNT15), (cite: ACCURSO17) and COMING (cite: Yasuda23), focused on galaxy-scale $\alpha_{\rm CO}$. Moreover, a survey of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ at fixed physical scale, which allows us to evaluate the environmental dependence of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ fairly, is also missing as previous spatially resolved studies (cite: LEROY11; SCHRUBA12; SANDSTROM13) tend to perform their analysis at fixed angular resolution. In this work, we will measure $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ across 37 nearby galaxies at a fixed $\sim$2 kpc resolution. This study is made possible by several surveys of resolved CO intensities in the past two decades: the Nobeyama CO Atlas of nearby galaxies (cite: Kuno07_NRO_CO), the HERA CO Line Extragalactic Survey (cite: LEROY09), the CO Multi-line Imaging of Nearby Galaxies project (cite: Sorai19_COMING), the Physics at High Angular resolution in Nearby Galaxies project (cite: Leroy21_PHANGS-ALMA_CO), and recent IRAM 30m observations (cite: Leroy21_CO_Line_Ratios).

This paper is presented as follows. In [2](#sec:calc_aco), we explain our methodology for deriving $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ from the data. We describe the data sets necessary for this work and how we constrain other physical quantities from observations in [3](#sec:data). We present the $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ measurements and their correlations with local and galaxy-integrated conditions in [4](#sec:results). In [5](#sec:aCO-SigmaMstar), we investigate an observed power-law relation between $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and $\Sigma_\star$ in the high-surface-density regions, and provide a prescription for $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ based on our findings. We discuss the physical interpretations of our results and how it compares to the literature findings in [6](#sec:discussions). Finally, we summarize our findings in [7](#sec:summary).

# Calculating $\alpha_{\rm CO}$

To calculate $\alpha_{\rm CO}$, we first estimate $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$ without using CO emission and an adopted conversion factor. In this study, we use a dust-based strategy to estimate $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$ by assuming a value for the fraction of metals locked in solid phase, i.e. the dust-to-metals ratio (D/M). The D/M is defined as: $$\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dtm}
    {\rm D/M} = \frac{\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{dust}}}{Z \times \ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}}},
\end{equation}$$ where $\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}}=\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{atom}}+ \ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}}$ is the total neutral gas surface density, $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$ is the molecular gas surface density, and the metallicity $Z$ converts $\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}$ to a “metal mass surface density”. By replacing $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$ in the above equation with the definition of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ in [\[eq:aco\]](#eq:aco), we have: $$\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aco_final}
    \ensuremath{\alpha_{\rm CO}}= \ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}}~W_\mathrm{CO}^{-1} = \Big(\frac{\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{dust}}}{Z\times \mathrm{(D/M)}}-\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{atom}}\Big){W_\mathrm{CO}^{-1}},
\end{equation}$$ where $\Sigma_\mathrm{dust}$, Z, $\Sigma_\mathrm{atom}$, and $W_\mathrm{CO}$ are measurable quantities, thus, by assigning a value of D/M, we can then calculate $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ with our data set. The uncertainty of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ is propagated from the uncertainties of $\Sigma_\mathrm{dust}$, metallicity, $\Sigma_\mathrm{atom}$, and $W_\mathrm{CO}$. The typical uncertainty of the pixel-by-pixel $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ measurements in this work is in the range of 0.2–0.5 dex[^2].

Dust-based $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ measurements in the literature usually have formulae similar with [\[eq:dtm\]](#eq:dtm) but with different assumptions. For example, (cite: ISRAEL97) and (cite: Leroy09_aCO) assumed a fixed dust-to-gas ratio (D/G) in their sample galaxies to derive $\alpha_{\rm CO}$. On the other hand, (cite: SANDSTROM13) assumed that the D/G remains approximately constant in a certain spatial region, e.g. kpc scale or entire galaxy. With this assumption, the authors are able to derive $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ by minimizing the scatter in D/G in a group of nearby pixels, treating $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and D/G as free parameters. This method has the advantage in not forcing the value of D/G and the disadvantage in sacrificing the spatial resolution.

Generally speaking, we could assume different D/M values in each pixel when we apply [\[eq:aco_final\]](#eq:aco_final). However, despite the previous efforts on studying the evolution of D/M (cite: DEVIS19; AOYAMA20_2020MNRAS.491.3844A; PerouxHowk20; Chiang21; Choban22; ROMAN-DUVAL22_METAL3), we do not have a well established prescription of how D/M depends on local environments, or the prescription is not more accurate than simply assuming a constant D/M. Studies have shown that at $\ensuremath{12+\log({\rm O/H})}> 8.2$, the D/M falls in the range[^3] between $0.4\mbox{--}0.7$, e.g. $0.5$ (cite: JENKINS09), $0.72$ (cite: LEROY11), $0.46$ (cite: REMY-RUYER14), $0.68$ (cite: DRAINE14), $0.7$ (cite: FELDMANN15), $0.56$ (cite: CHIANG18), and $0.40\mbox{--}0.58$ (cite: Chiang21). Meanwhile, studies have shown that in galaxy centers, $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ can vary by a factor of 10 (cite: SANDSTROM13; BOLATTO13; Israel20; Teng22; Teng23), which is a significantly larger dynamic range than D/M. In the following, we will take a constant $\mathrm{D/M}=0.55$ (mean of 0.4–0.7) as the fiducial case for deriving $\alpha_{\rm CO}$. A possible drawback by assuming a constant D/M is that D/M has been shown to decrease toward lower metallicity (cite: REMY-RUYER14; HIRASHITA11; CHIANG18; DEVIS19). Thus, the assumed D/M value that is appropriate for galaxy centers is likely too high for low-metallicity regions (usually the outer disks), resulting in an underestimation of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$([\[eq:aco_final\]](#eq:aco_final)) in the outer disk. We will discuss the case of a varying D/M with a toy model in [8](#app:d/m). We will also discuss the possible uncertainties in $\Sigma_\mathrm{dust}$ derivation in [3](#sec:data).

## CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ and CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ cases

In this multi-wavelength, multi-galaxy study, we do not always have both the lowest-$J$ CO emission lines for all the target galaxies. Studies have been using CO line ratios to convert the intensity between CO emission lines. For an in-depth discussion on low-$J$ CO line ratios, we refer the readers to (cite: Leroy21_CO_Line_Ratios). In the literature, perhaps the most frequently used method to treat different CO line coverage is converting everything to $W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ with a constant CO line ratio (cite: SANDSTROM13; Sun20; Chiang21). This method allows us to uniformly use $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ for calculating $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$ in the study. Theoretically, the line ratio can vary with excitation conditions like gas temperature and linewidth. Thus, we expect $R_{21}$ to trace the local environmental conditions. Taking the line ratio for $W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ and $W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ as an example: $$\begin{equation}
R_{21} \equiv \frac{\ensuremath{W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}}{\ensuremath{W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}},
\end{equation}$$ where $R_{21}$ is usually falls in the range of 0.3 to 0.9 with mean value $\sim 0.65$ for normal star-forming galaxies, and it is expected to be higher in galaxy centers (cite: LEROY09; Leroy21_CO_Line_Ratios; Leroy23_JWST-CO; denBrok21; Yajima21).

In this work, however, we will not adopt the simple strategy as our fiducial case because most of our target galaxies have CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ data, that $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ has attained its own importance due to modern observations, and that the variation in $R_{21}$ is non-negligible. We will present four solutions of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ in parallel, two without any conversions between CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ and CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$, and two with different prescriptions of the line ratio:

1.  $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ calculated with $W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ data only.

2.  $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ calculated with $W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ data only.

3.  $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ calculated with $W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ data, plus $W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ for galaxies without $W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ data, converted with a constant $R_{21}$.

4.  $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ calculated with $W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ data, plus $W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ for galaxies without $W_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ data, converted with an environment-dependent $R_{21}$.

For the third method, we adopt the constant $R_{21}=0.65$ from (cite: Leroy21_CO_Line_Ratios). For the last method, we adopt the MIR-dependent formula suggested by (cite: Leroy23_JWST-CO), namely $$\begin{equation}
\label{eq: R21(W4)}
    R_{21} = 0.62\left(\frac{I_\mathrm{WISE4}}{1\,{\rm MJy\,sr\textsuperscript{-1}}}\right)^{0.22}.
\end{equation}$$ We follow the suggestion in (cite: Leroy23_JWST-CO) and cap $R_{21}$ at $R_{21}=1$. This formula in general agrees with the finding that $R_{21}$ scales with MIR intensity or $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$ with a power-law index $\sim 0.15$–$0.2$ (cite: denBrok21; Yajima21; Leroy21_CO_Line_Ratios; Leroy23_JWST-CO).

# Data

We measure $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ in 37 nearby galaxies in this study. To measure $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ with our dust-based methodology ([2](#sec:calc_aco)), the data sets required are dust surface density ($\Sigma_\mathrm{dust}$, from IR SED modelling), CO low-$J$ rotational line integrated intensity ($W_\mathrm{CO}$), atomic gas surface density ($\Sigma_\mathrm{atom}$, from H I 21 cm line emission), and metallicity ($Z$, from gas-phase oxygen abundance in H II regions). We first select our sample galaxies from the dust catalog of $z$=0 Multiwavelength Galaxy Synthesis ($z$0MGS) (cite: LEROY19; Chastenet21_M101). From this large sample, we pick the 49 galaxies with both low-$J$ CO rotational line and H I data available, including our own new H I data sets. We design our study with a common resolution of 2 kpc, which draws a limit in sample selection at distance $\sim 20~$Mpc since the worst resolution data in our sample usually have angular resolution around $20\ensuremath{''}$. High-inclination ($>80^\circ$) targets are also excluded. We further exclude 4 galaxies[^4] that satisfy all above conditions but do not satisfy the signal-to-noise ratio conditions that will be described in [3.3](#sec:data:masking and completeness). The selection yields 37 galaxies in our sample. We list the properties of these galaxies in [1](#tab:samples).

## Physical Quantities and Data Sets

**Dust properties.** We obtain dust properties by fitting the dust emission spectral energy distribution (SED) to the (cite: DRAINE07) physical dust model. The details of the IR data processing and dust SED fitting are reported in (cite: Chastenet21_M101) and J. Chastenet et al. (in preparation). We briefly summarize the process below.

We obtain the dust emission SED in the IR observed by two space telescopes: the 3.4, 4.6, 12 and 22 $\mu$m bands with the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (cite: WRIGHT10), and the 70, 100, 160 and 250 $\mu$m bands with the *Herschel Space Observatory* (cite: PILBRATT10). The *Herschel* and WISE maps are first convolved to SPIRE 250 PSF and then to a 21$''$ Gaussian PSF using the SPIRE 250-to-Gauss-21$''$ kernel from (cite: ANIANO11). The 21$''$ PSF is the “moderate” Gaussian from (cite: ANIANO11) that provides relatively high angular resolution without amplifying image artifacts. Finally, these maps are convolved to the desired resolution: a Gaussian PSF with spatial resolution corresponding to FWHM of 2 kpc.

After convolving the IR maps, we fit the dust SED with the (cite: DRAINE07) physical dust model with the dust opacity calibration derived in (cite: Chastenet21_M101). This calibration is based on metallicity measured with “direct” electron-temperature-based methods, which is consistent with the strong lien calibration adopted in this work (cite: PilyuginGrebel16), and yields reasonable D/M. Thus, the calibration ties dust opacity, D/M and metallicity into one framework. The complete set of data products from the fitting includes the maps of dust mass surface density ($\Sigma_\mathrm{dust}$), interstellar radiation field (the minimum radiation field $U_\mathrm{min}$ and the fraction of dust heated by the power-law radiation field $\gamma$) and the fractional dust mass in the form of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons ($\rm q_{PAH}$). The maximum radiation field is fixed at $U_{\rm max}=10^7$ and the power-law index for radiation field distribution is fixed at $\alpha=2$. From the fitted $U_\mathrm{min}$ and $\gamma$, we can derive the dust-mass-averaged radiation field $\overline{U}$, which is the fiducial tracer for radiation field in this work.

We also note that we assume fixed dust properties in our dust SED fitting throughout this study, which is the most frequently adopted strategy in the literature. The accuracy of $\Sigma_\mathrm{dust}$ estimates, derived by fitting the IR SED with dust emission models, can be affected by variations in the dust opacity. Interstellar dust grains are not uniform in their chemical composition, size distribution, and shape, leading to variations in their opacity (cite: DRAINE07; HirashitaVoshchinnikov14; DraineHensley21). In the MW, (cite: Stepnik03) found that the dust opacity increases by $\sim 3$ times from the diffuse ISM to the dense clouds. The authors argued that the increase in dust opacity is resulted from the deficit of small grains due to grain-grain coagulation. It is challenging to measure the variation in opacity of interstellar dust since it is degenerate with the environmental dependence of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and D/M. Moreover, many of the mechanisms that affects dust opacity, e.g. grain-grain coagulation and ice mantles, are smoothed out in kpc-scale extra-galactic studies (cite: GALLIANO18), meaning that its variation is likely less observable than the other degenerate factors like $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and D/M. We note that there are extra-galactic studies that attribute all the variations in dust and gas properties to dust opacity to evaluate its variation, e.g. (cite: CLARK19_2019MNRAS.489.5256C) found that dust opacity change by a factor $\sim 2$ within M74 and $\sim 5$ within M83.\
**Atomic gas surface density.** We trace the atomic gas surface density ($\Sigma_\mathrm{atom}$) with the H I 21 cm integrated intensity ($I_\textsc{H\,i}$), assuming the opacity is negligible (cite: WALTER08): $$\begin{equation}
\label{eq:hi}
    \frac{\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{atom}}}{1~\ensuremath{\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}}} = 
    1.36\times(1.46\times10^{-2})\times \frac{W_\textsc{H\,i}}{1~{\rm K\,km\,s\textsuperscript{-1}}}~,
\end{equation}$$ where the $1.36$ factor accounts for the mass of helium.

We obtain $W_\textsc{H\,i}$ from both literature and new data, as listed in [1](#tab:samples). The two new H I surveys are the EveryTHINGS survey (P.I. K. M. Sandstrom; I. Chiang et al. in preparation) and the PHANGS-VLA survey (P.I. D. Utomo). The EveryTHINGS survey targets nearby galaxies with *Herschel* photometric data but without high-resolution H I observations, while the PHANGS-VLA survey focuses on galaxies in the Physics at High Angular resolution in Nearby Galaxies (PHANGS) project[^5]. Both surveys have their data observed with the C- and D-configurations of *Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA)*[^6], which yield an angular resolutions in the range of $20\ensuremath{''}$ to $30\ensuremath{''}$. Both surveys provide new high-sensitivity 21 cm H I observations in tens of nearby galaxies. We did not include WHISP (cite: Swaters02_WHISP) data because the galaxies that only have WHISP data have resolution coarser than 2 kpc after convolving to a circular PSF.\
**CO low-$J$ rotational lines.** The integrated intensity of CO low-$J$ rotational lines traces the molecular gas surface density ([\[eq:aco\]](#eq:aco)), and is key to this study. We use the compilation of CO mapping assembled by (cite: Leroy21_CO_Line_Ratios; Leroy23_JWST-CO) from several publicly available CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ and CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ data:

- CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ data from the COMING survey (cite: Sorai19_COMING) and the CO Atlas (cite: Kuno07_NRO_CO).

- CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ data from HERACLES (cite: LEROY09), the PHANGS-ALMA survey (cite: Leroy21_PHANGS-ALMA_CO), and a new survey observed by the IRAM-30m focused on the Virgo Cluster (cite: Leroy21_CO_Line_Ratios).

The source of CO data for each galaxy is listed in [1](#tab:samples), where CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ and CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ are listed separately. All these literature measurements focus on the $^{12}\mathrm{C}^{16}\mathrm{O}$ isotopologue, hereafter CO for simplicity.\
**Surface densities of stellar mass and SFR.** We trace the surface densities of stellar mass and SFR ($\Sigma_\star$ and $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$, respectively) using the data and conversion formulae presented in the $z$0MGS survey (cite: LEROY19). We utilize the $z$0MGS compilation of the background-subtracted WISE (cite: WRIGHT10) $\lambda\sim3.4$ and 22 $\mu$m (hereafter WISE1 and WISE4, respectively) data and the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (cite: MARTIN05) $\lambda\sim154~\rm nm$ (hereafter FUV) data.

We use WISE1 data to trace stellar mass surface density ($\Sigma_\star$) with: $$\begin{equation}
\frac{\ensuremath{\Sigma_\star}}{1~\ensuremath{\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}}} = 3.3 \times 10^2 \left(\frac{\Upsilon^{3.4}_\star}{0.5~\mathrm{M_\odot~L_\odot^{-1}}}\right) \frac{I_{\rm WISE1}}{1~{\rm MJy\,sr\textsuperscript{-1}}}~,
\end{equation}$$ where $\Upsilon^{3.4}_\star$ is the $\Sigma_\star$-to-WISE1 mass-to-light ratio. The value of $\Upsilon^{3.4}_\star$ is calculated from the galaxy-by-galaxy SFR-to-WISE1 ratio, a “specific SFR-like” quantity, with the prescription calibrated in Appendix A of (cite: LEROY19).

We use FUV and WISE4 data to trace the SFR surface density ($\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$) also with the conversion formula suggested by $z$0MGS (cite: LEROY19; Belfiore23). For galaxies with both FUV and WISE4 available, we use: $$\begin{multline}
\frac{\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}}}{1~\ensuremath{{\rm M_\odot\,yr}^{-1}\,{\rm kpc}^{-2}}} = \\
8.85 \times 10^{-2} \frac{I_{\rm FUV}}{1~{\rm MJy\,sr\textsuperscript{-1}}} + 3.02 \times 10^{-3} \frac{I_{\rm WISE4}}{1~{\rm MJy\,sr\textsuperscript{-1}}}~.
\end{multline}$$

For NGC3953 and NGC4689, where only WISE4 is available, we use: $$\begin{equation}
\frac{\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}}}{1~\ensuremath{{\rm M_\odot\,yr}^{-1}\,{\rm kpc}^{-2}}} =
3.81 \times 10^{-3} \frac{I_{\rm W4}}{1~{\rm MJy\,sr\textsuperscript{-1}}}~.
\end{equation}$$

For both WISE and GALEX maps, we blank the regions with foreground stars identified in the $z$0MGS database. We interpolate the intensities in the blanked region with a Gaussian kernel FWHM = 22.5$''$ (the adopted WISE and GALEX maps have FWHM = 15$''$) with the function `interpolate_replace_nans` in `astropy.convolution`. This interpolation is done on the maps before any convolution, reprojection, or unit conversion. Regarding the WISE maps, this treatment is only done for the maps used for calculating $\Sigma_\star$ and $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$. For the WISE maps used in dust SED fitting, we refer the readers to J. Chastenet et al. (in preparation).\
**Specific SFR.** With the measurements of $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$ and $\Sigma_\star$, we calculate the specific SFR (sSFR) as: $$\begin{equation}
    \frac{\rm sSFR}{\rm 1~yr^{-1}} = 1 \times 10^{-6} \times
\big(\bm{\sum}_i\frac{\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}}}{1~\ensuremath{{\rm M_\odot\,yr}^{-1}\,{\rm kpc}^{-2}}}\big)\big(\bm{\sum}_i\frac{\ensuremath{\Sigma_\star}}{1~\ensuremath{\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}}}\big)^{-1},
\end{equation}$$ where $\bm{\sum}_i$ is the summation over pixels in a galaxy. Meanwhile, we calculate the spatially resolved sSFR (rsSFR) as: $$\begin{equation}
    \frac{\rm rsSFR}{\rm 1~yr^{-1}} = 1 \times 10^{-6} \times
\frac{\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}}}{1~\ensuremath{{\rm M_\odot\,yr}^{-1}\,{\rm kpc}^{-2}}}\big(\frac{\ensuremath{\Sigma_\star}}{1~\ensuremath{\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}}}\big)^{-1}.
\end{equation}$$

**Metallicity.** We use the abundance of oxygen, $12+\log({\rm O/H})$, to trace the metallicity ($Z$). We assume a fixed abundance pattern, i.e. a constant oxygen-to-total-metal mass ratio. The conversion from $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ to $Z$ then becomes: $$\begin{equation}
    Z = 0.0134 \times 10^{\ensuremath{12+\log({\rm O/H})}- 8.69},
\end{equation}$$ where 0.0134 and 8.69 are the adopted $Z_\odot$ and $\ensuremath{12+\log({\rm O/H})}_\odot$, respectively (cite: ASPLUND09).

We calculate $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ for each pixel as a function of the galactocentric distance by adopting the radial gradient of $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ derived from measurements in H II regions. We use data from two surveys: the PHANGS-MUSE survey (cite: Emsellem22_PHANGS-MUSE; Groves23) and the (cite: Zurita21) compilation. We use the (cite: PilyuginGrebel16) S-calibration[^7] (hereafter PG16S) as the fiducial calibration for $12+\log({\rm O/H})$. PG16S is a calibration method that shows good agreement with direct metallicity measurements (cite: CROXALL16; Kreckel19). Since PG16S only relies on lines covered by MUSE, the $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ measurement can be expanded to the full PHANGS-MUSE dataset in our future works.

For galaxies in the PHANGS-MUSE survey, we adopt radial $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ gradients presented in (cite: Santoro22), which are calculated with the PG16S calibration. For galaxies that only appear in the (cite: Zurita21) emission data compilation, we use the (cite: Zurita21) data to calculate the PG16S $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ and then fit the radial $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ gradient in these galaxies. We only consider galaxies that have at least 5 measurements spanning at least $0.5R_{25}$ in the (cite: Zurita21) data table. The uncertainties of the $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ gradient is not explicitly provided in either work. We will assume a 0.1 dex scatter for $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ derived from gradients as suggested in (cite: Berg20).

For galaxies without measurements of $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ in either (cite: Zurita21) or (cite: Santoro22), we use the two-step strategy proposed in (cite: Sun20) to estimate their $12+\log({\rm O/H})$. First, we use a mass-metallicity relation to predict $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ at one effective radius ($R_\mathrm{e}$) in a given galaxy. Second, we extend the prediction with a radial gradient of $-0.1~\mathrm{dex}/R_\mathrm{e}$ suggested by (cite: Sanchez14). We characterize the mass-metallicity with a function of the form: $$\begin{equation}
    \ensuremath{12+\log({\rm O/H})}= a + bxe^{-x},
\end{equation}$$ where $x=\log(M_\star/\mathrm{M}_\odot) - 11.5$ (cite: Sanchez19). $a$ and $b$ are free parameters. We fit the function with $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ at one $\rm R_e$ from galaxies with the available measurements listed in [1](#tab:samples). The best-fit parameters are $a=8.56\pm 0.02$ and $b=0.010\pm0.002$, which are robust under resampling. Meanwhile, the typical statistical uncertainty in the $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ data used for fitting is $\sim 0.013$ dex. However, the root mean square error ($\Delta_\mathrm{rms}$) between the best fit and data is 0.13 dex, meaning that there is still intrinsic scatter in $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ that is not explained by the mass-metallicity relation and the adopted radial gradients, e.g. the azimuthal variations (cite: Williams22_Metal2D). We use this fitted relation to derive the radial metallicity gradient of galaxies without metallicity measurements with the $M_\star$ and $R_\mathrm{e}$ listed in [1](#tab:samples). We will assume an uncertainty of 0.15 dex (rounding up $0.013+0.13$ dex) for galaxies with this type of $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ measurements.

Studies have reported that the PG16S calibration could result in $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ value lower than other calibrations (cite: DEVIS19). Aligning with that, there are also studies reporting that the $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ calibrated with PG16S in Orion Nebula and other H II regions in the solar neighborhood have values $\sim0.2$ dex lower than the solar reference value (cite: Esteban22). This effect could lead to an underestimate of Z’ and thus an overestimate in $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ with our methodology. For consistency with the direct metallicity calibration used in (cite: Chastenet21_M101) for calibrating dust opacity, we will use PG16S in this work.

## Uniform Data Processing

The analyses in this work are done at a common resolution of 2 kpc for all data. For H I, CO, $\Sigma_\star$, and $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$, we convolve them to a circular Gaussian PSF with a FWHM corresponding to 2 kpc, using the `astropy.convolution` package (cite: ASTROPY13; Astropy18; Astropy22). The images are then reprojected onto a grid with a pixel size of one third of the FWHM (that is, we oversample at roughly the Nyquist sampling rate) with the `astropy` affiliated package `reproject`. The convolution and reprojection of the dust maps are done in J. Chastenet et al. (in preparation). They convolve the IR maps into the final resolution using kernels from (cite: ANIANO11). Note that the convolution is done before SED fitting for dust properties. The galactocentric radius and metallicity are directly calculated on the final pixel grids. All the surface density and surface brightness quantities presented in this work have been corrected for inclination, listed in [1](#tab:samples).

## S/N Mask and Completeness

**S/N Mask.** For statistical quantities that only involve $\alpha_{\rm CO}$, e.g. mean values and percentiles, we masked out the low signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) pixels. Specifically, we blank pixels with $\mathrm{S/N} < 1$ in $W_\mathrm{CO}$ and $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$. Note that $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$ here is derived from $\Sigma_\mathrm{dust}$(with IR photometry), metallicity and $\Sigma_\mathrm{atom}$([\[eq:aco_final\]](#eq:aco_final)), thus the uncertainty of $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$ is propagated from the uncertainties of these three quantities and the IR photometry.\
**Completeness.** For statistical quantities that involve $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and another quantity ($X$), e.g. correlations and linear regression, in addition to the S/N mask, we only calculate with data with high ($>50\%$) completeness in $X$ as the trend confidence criteria. The completeness for data with $X_i \leq X < X_f$, or $[X_i,~X_f)$, is defined as: $$\begin{equation}
    Completeness \equiv \frac{{\rm num~of~S/N~>~1}~pixels~with~[X_i,~X_f)}{{\rm num~of~all~pixels~with}~[X_i,~X_f)},
\end{equation}$$ where the definition of “S/N \> 1” is the same as the S/N mask earlier this subsection. We show the completeness and the $50\%$ threshold in our data set in [1](#fig:aCO10_completeness). For most quantities, the CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ data has a better completeness coverage than the CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ data. Note that at the high-$\overline{U}$ end, the completeness fluctuates around 50%. We treat all data with $\log\ensuremath{\overline{U}}>0.75$ as incomplete for simplicity.

In total, we measure resolved $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ values across 37 galaxies, including $\sim790$ and $\sim610$ independent measurements[^8] from CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ and CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ data, respectively. We summarize the measurements in [\[tab:aco_stats\]](#tab:aco_stats) and the distribution of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ in [2](#fig:aCO_hist). For each galaxy, we report the mean, CO-intensity-weighted mean, 16$^{\rm th}$-84$^{\rm th}$ percentiles, and number of pixel-by-pixel measurements of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$.

The mean value for $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$ and $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$ are 9.3 and 4.2 ${\rm M_\odot\,pc^{-2}\,(K\,km\,s^{-1})^{-1}}$ with 16$^{\rm th}$-84$^{\rm th}$ percentiles spanning 3.9–14.0 and 2.2–6.1 ${\rm M_\odot\,pc^{-2}\,(K\,km\,s^{-1})^{-1}}$, respectively. The mean $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$ corresponds to $\sim0.97 \ensuremath{\alpha_{\rm CO}^{\rm MW}}$, whereas the mean $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$ corresponds to $\sim1.39 \ensuremath{\alpha_{\rm CO}^{\rm MW}}$ assuming a constant $R_{21}=0.65$.

Besides the simple mean, we also calculate the $W_{\rm CO}$-weighted mean, which better reflects the $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ value to be adopted for data at coarser resolution. The $W_{\rm CO}$-weighted mean for $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$ and $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$ are 5.69 and 3.33, respectively. Both values are lower than the simple mean, which indicates that the $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ values are lower in brighter regions. Unless specified otherwise, we use $W_\mathrm{CO}$-weighted mean $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ for galaxy-integrated analysis in the following content.

When we include CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ data for galaxies without CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ measurements with a variable $R_{21}$ (values with  in [\[tab:aco_stats\]](#tab:aco_stats)), the mean and $W_{\rm CO}$-weighted mean of $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$ increase to 4.72 and 3.48, respectively, indicating that galaxies without CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ measurements in this data set tend to have larger $\alpha_{\rm CO}$. This is also visualized in the bottom panel of [2](#fig:aCO_hist). Also, we find that the distribution of $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$ does not differ much between the two $R_{21}$ prescriptions adopted in this work: the fixed $R_{21}=0.65$ and the $I_{\rm W4}$-dependent $R_{21}$.

In [\[tab:aco_stats\]](#tab:aco_stats), we also list the $W_\mathrm{CO}$ recovery fraction ($W_\mathrm{CO}\%$), which is the percentage of $W_\mathrm{CO}$ recovered (above the S/N mask) in the pixel-by-pixel analysis in each galaxy. We notice a few galaxies with low $W_\mathrm{CO}$ recovery fraction, meaning that there are significant numbers of pixels with $W_\mathrm{CO}$ detection removed from analysis. The main reason for NGC3631 and most galaxies with recovery fraction above 50% is low sensitivity in dust/IR data. In NGC3631, $>85\%$ of pixels removed have ${\rm S/N} < 1$ in the IR bands. In NGC3198 and NGC4625, the sensitivity in dust/IR only explains $<60\%$ of pixels removed. The rest of the pixels were removed due to ${\rm S/N} < 1$ in $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$, a combined effect of $\Sigma_\mathrm{dust}$, $\Sigma_\mathrm{atom}$ and $12+\log({\rm O/H})$. This type of pixels have ${\rm S/N} > 1$ in $W_\mathrm{CO}$ and ${\rm S/N} < 1$ in $\Sigma_\mathrm{mol}$, likely indicating a small $\alpha_{\rm CO}$.

: The correlation and linear regression between pixel-by-pixel $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ measurements and local physical quantities.

![](aCO21_properties.pdf)

![](aCO10_properties.pdf)

We measure the pixel-by-pixel correlations between $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and several parameters describing local physical conditions. These results are summarized in [2](#tab: aCO_prop) and visualized in [3](#fig:aCO21_properties)-[4](#fig:aCO10_properties). Note that the correlations and linear regressions[^9] are calculated with data in the complete zone only (with data completeness $>50\%$; see [3.3](#sec:data:masking and completeness) for details). The errorbars in [3](#fig:aCO21_properties)-[4](#fig:aCO10_properties) include both the scatter within a bin and the uncertainties of pixel-by-pixel measurements. We first bootstrap the measurements by 1000 times with uncertainties, and then sample the 16th- and 84-percentiles in each bin from the bootstrapped sample as the errorbars. We apply the same method for visualizing the other binned data in this work.

As shown in [2](#tab: aCO_prop), most quantities have significant correlations ($p$-value \< 0.05) with $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ except $\Sigma_\star$. $\Sigma_\star$ has significant correlations with $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$ from CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ data only and $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$ from CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ only, but not when we combine CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ and CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ data. This is likely due to the negative $\Sigma_\star$-to-$\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$ and the positive $\Sigma_\star$-to-$\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$ correlations, although both of which are weak.

$\log\ensuremath{\overline{U}}$ has the strongest negative correlation with $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$, meaning that $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$ decreases toward regions with stronger interstellar radiation field strength. This is consistent with the picture that $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ decreases with higher gas temperature and larger line width (cite: BOLATTO13). It is also the case that a higher $\log\ensuremath{\overline{U}}$ might correspond to a lower $\Sigma_\mathrm{dust}$ as a caveat of our fitting methodology (cite: SHETTY09; SHETTY09B). However, since we do not see a strong $\Sigma_\mathrm{dust}$-to-$\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$ correlation, the above effect should be minor. Several other quantities also show moderate (negative) correlations with $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$, i.e. $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$ and rsSFR. Studies have shown strong correlations between $\log\ensuremath{\overline{U}}$ and $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$(cite: Hirashita_Chiang22; Chiang23). Another quantity that shows moderate correlation is $W_\mathrm{CO}$. $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ is expected to anti-correlate with $W_\mathrm{CO}$ due to either external pressure or other dynamical effects (cite: BOLATTO13; Sun18). The power-law index for $W_\mathrm{CO}$ is within the previously reported range of $-0.32$ to $-0.54$ (cite: NARAYANAN12; Gong20; Hunt23).

Compared to $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$, the correlations between $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$ and local conditions are overall weaker. $\log~{\rm rsSFR}$ has the strongest correlation with $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$ in all three $R_{21}$ cases, and $\log\ensuremath{\overline{U}}$ is the second strongest.

For all combinations of $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\rm CO}}$ and local conditions, we perform linear regression with the functional form: $$\begin{equation}
    \log\ensuremath{\alpha_{\rm CO}}=mx+b,
\end{equation}$$ where $x$[^10] is the local condition and both $m$ and $b$ are free parameters, all of which are listed in [2](#tab: aCO_prop). In the same table, we also report the root-mean-square error ($\Delta_\mathrm{rms}$) between the measured and fitted $\log\ensuremath{\alpha_{\rm CO}}$. Most formulas have $\ensuremath{\Delta_\mathrm{rms}}\sim 0.2$ dex. $W_\mathrm{CO}$, $\overline{U}$ and $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$ have the strongest correlations and smallest $\Delta_\mathrm{rms}$ in general.

One quantity that is often used for parametrizing $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ is $12+\log({\rm O/H})$. In our measurements, $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ has moderate to weak correlation with $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ in all cases. The slope from linear regression ($m$) is $-2.6$ for $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$ and $-1.8$ to $-2.3$ for $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$. These values are mildly steeper than most literature values (cite: BOLATTO13; HUNT15; ACCURSO17; Sun20), but are still within previous reported range, e.g. $-2.0$ to $-2.8$ in (cite: SCHRUBA12). Note that our data set is less suitable for an in-depth study on $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ since $>80\%$ of our data is concentrated in a small dynamic range of $8.4 \leq \ensuremath{12+\log({\rm O/H})}\leq 8.6$.

We also calculate the correlation between physical quantities and normalized $\alpha_{\rm CO}$. In this calculation, $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ is normalized by the $W_\mathrm{CO}$-weighted mean in each galaxy. For most quantities, the correlation become weaker after normalization. Meanwhile, $\Sigma_\star$ has a stronger correlation with normalized $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ in all cases in [2](#tab: aCO_prop), indicating that $\Sigma_\star$ traces the intra-galaxy $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ variations after normalization of galaxy-to-galaxy differences.

Overall, we have shown that $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$ has stronger correlations with local conditions than $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$. Among the local quantities, $W_\mathrm{CO}$, $\overline{U}$, and $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$ usually have stronger correlations with $\alpha_{\rm CO}$. We do not see a strong correlation coefficient between $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and $12+\log({\rm O/H})$, one of the most frequently used quantity to model $\alpha_{\rm CO}$.

## Correlation with Galaxy-Averaged Quantities

![](mean_aCO21_properties.pdf)

![](mean_aCO10_properties.pdf)

Besides kpc-scale variations, we also test how galaxy-averaged $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$ and $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$ vary between galaxies, and how their variations correlate with galaxy-averaged properties. The results are visualized in [5](#fig:mean_aCO21_properties)-[6](#fig:mean_aCO10_properties). We use the symbol $\text{<}X\text{>}$ to represent the simple averaged value of quantity $X$ in each galaxy, i.e. $\Sigma_i^{\rm gal} X_i / \Sigma_i^{\rm gal}$, where $\Sigma_i^{\rm gal}$ is the summation over all pixels in a galaxy. There are three quantities for which we do not apply simple averages: (1) as mentioned in [4](#sec:results), we will present the $W_\mathrm{CO}$-weighted mean of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$; (2) $\log\ensuremath{\overline{U}}_\mathrm{gal}$ is calculated as $\log \big(\Sigma_i^{\rm gal}\Sigma_{{\rm dust},i} \ensuremath{\overline{U}}_i/\Sigma_i^{\rm gal}\Sigma_{{\rm dust},i}$) to reflect the dust-mass-weighted averaged ISRF; (3) sSFR is calculated as $\Sigma_i^{\rm gal}\Sigma_{{\rm SFR},i}/\Sigma_i^{\rm gal}\Sigma_{\star,i}=SFR/M_\star$. The errorbars in [5](#fig:mean_aCO21_properties)-[6](#fig:mean_aCO10_properties) show the 16th-84th percentiles of the corresponding quantity. In [6](#fig:mean_aCO10_properties), we also include $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$ calculated with CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ data with a $I_\mathrm{W4}$-dependent $R_{21}$. We only include one $R_{21}$ prescription here for clarity.

We report the correlation coefficients and the corresponding $p$-values in each panel of [5](#fig:mean_aCO21_properties)-[6](#fig:mean_aCO10_properties). Compared to the results in [4.1](#sec:results:local), we note that whether a quantity has significant correlation with $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and the strength of the correlation often differ between the spatially resolved case and the galaxy-averaged case. Several quantities show significant correlations with \<$\alpha_\mathrm{CO}$\>. $12+\log({\rm O/H})$ and \<$\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$\> seem to show stronger correlation with \<$\alpha_\mathrm{CO}$\> for both CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ and CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ than in the spatially resolved case. The insignificant correlation between \<$\Sigma_{\star}$\> and $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ is consistent with the findings in (cite: Carleton17) and (cite: Dunne22) assuming that $\Sigma_\star$ dominates the total mass surface density and that CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ dominates the CO measurements.

# Power-law dependence of the conversion factor on stellar mass surface density

![](aCO_first.pdf)

In the $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ prescription proposed in (cite: BOLATTO13), the authors use a power law with $\Sigma_\mathrm{Total}$(=$\Sigma_\star$+$\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}$) to trace the changes in $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ due to CO emissivity variations (related to gas temperature and opacity) and a threshold in $\Sigma_\mathrm{Total}$ to trace where the effects become important. Inspired by their work and motivated by the necessity of improving $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ prescriptions in galaxy centers, we examine whether a similar functional form applies to our $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ measurements. Furthermore, as shown in the previous section, the correlation between $\Sigma_\star$ and $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ improves after normalizing $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ the their $W_\mathrm{CO}$-weighted mean, which could fit into the picture of separating CO-dark and starburst components in (cite: BOLATTO13). With the WISE full-sky observations, the resolved $\Sigma_\star$ for all nearby galaxies is widely available, which makes this kind of prescription easy to apply. In this study, we will focus on the $\alpha_{\rm CO}$-to-$\Sigma_\star$ relation instead of $\Sigma_\mathrm{Total}$ because our data set is mostly $\Sigma_\star$-dominated (50% with $\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}}/\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{Total}}<0.2$; 99.5% with $\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{gas}}/\ensuremath{\Sigma_\mathrm{Total}}<0.5$).

We present the correlations between $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and $\Sigma_\star$ in [7](#fig:aCO_first) for both $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$ (left panels) and $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$ (right panels). In the top panels, we present the profile of measured $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ versus $\Sigma_\star$ in each galaxy. For $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}}$, most galaxies have their $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ anti-correlate with $\Sigma_\star$ at $\ensuremath{\Sigma_\star}>100~\ensuremath{\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}}$ aside from a few exceptions. It is similar for $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}}$, but with a flatter $\alpha_{\rm CO}$-to-$\Sigma_\star$ slope. At the low-$\Sigma_\star$ end, some galaxies still have negative $\alpha_{\rm CO}$-to-$\Sigma_\star$ correlations while the others have strong positive correlations. In the middle panels, we show the collective behavior across galaxies using a binned average as a function of $\Sigma_\star$, with each bin spanning $\sim 0.1$ dex in $\Sigma_\star$.

We find that in regions with high-$\Sigma_\star$, $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ generally decreases with $\Sigma_\star$, which is consistent with the negative power-law index in the (cite: BOLATTO13) formula. There appears to be galaxy-to-galaxy variation in the value of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$, but good agreement in the rate of how fast $\ensuremath{\alpha_{\rm CO}}$ decreases with $\ensuremath{\Sigma_\star}$. To better illustrate this phenomena, we normalize $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ in each galaxy at a threshold $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}}\equiv 100~\ensuremath{\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}}$ (cite: BOLATTO13) and show the normalized $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ in the bottom panel of [7](#fig:aCO_first). The normalization in each galaxy ($\alpha_{\rm CO,gal,T}$) is defined as the median $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ of pixels with their $\Sigma_\star$ within $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}}\pm 0.05$ dex.

In the remainder of this section, we will focus on analyzing the scaling relation between $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and $\Sigma_\star$ in a sub-sample of galaxies with at least 5 measurements with $\ensuremath{\Sigma_\star}> \ensuremath{\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}}$ (29 galaxies for CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ and 25 galaxies for CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$, see the $\rm N_{pix,100}$ column in [\[tab:aco_stats\]](#tab:aco_stats)). We use a power law to characterize this scaling relation: $$\begin{equation}
\label{eq:power law}
    \log \frac{\ensuremath{\alpha_{\rm CO}}}{\ensuremath{\alpha_{\rm CO,gal,T}}} = a\times\log\frac{\ensuremath{\Sigma_\star}}{\ensuremath{\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}}} + b,~\ensuremath{\Sigma_\star}\geq\ensuremath{\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}},
\end{equation}$$ where $a$ (the power-law index) and $b$ (the offset) are free parameters. Since both $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and $\Sigma_\star$ are normalized in the formula, we expect $b\sim 0$ (and $b_\mathrm{gal}\sim 0$) if $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ monotonically decreases with $\Sigma_\star$. By default, we fit [\[eq:power law\]](#eq:power law) with all data. When fitting data in individual galaxies only, we will describe the parameters as $a_\mathrm{gal}$ and $b_\mathrm{gal}$.

We exclude data from galaxies that do not satisfy the following criteria: (1) at least 5 measurements at $\ensuremath{\Sigma_\star}>\ensuremath{\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}}$; (2) spanning at least 0.1 dex in $\Sigma_\star$ at $\ensuremath{\Sigma_\star}>\ensuremath{\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}}$. Since all criteria are $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$-dependent, we expect the size of sub-sample space to vary with $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$. We will visualize the galaxies not satisfying the last two criteria in [5.2](#sec:aCO-SigmaMstar:galaxy).

With the fiducial setting, i.e. $\mathrm{D/M}=0.55$ and $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}}=100~\ensuremath{\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}}$, the fitting yields $a=-0.50^{+0.07}_{-0.06}$ and $b=0.03^{+0.01}_{-0.01}$ with $\ensuremath{\Delta_\mathrm{rms}}=0.15~\mathrm{dex}$ for CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$; $a=-0.22^{+0.06}_{-0.06}$ and $b=0.003^{+0.01}_{-0.01}$ with $\ensuremath{\Delta_\mathrm{rms}}=0.13~\mathrm{dex}$ for CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$[^11]. The small $b$ values, which are consistent with our expectations, indicate that the $\alpha_{\rm CO}$-to-$\Sigma_\star$ relation matches with the picture of a simple power law. The difference between the $a$ values for CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$ and CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$ data is consistent with the finding that $R_{21} \propto I_\mathrm{MIR}^{-0.2}$ (cite: Leroy23_JWST-CO). The uncertainties of $a$ and $b$ are estimated from 1000 rounds of bootstrap resampling. In each round, we select 29 (25) galaxies for CO $(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)$(CO $(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)$) data with replacement from our sample galaxies to fit the power law. We then take the difference between the best-fit parameter and the 84th- (16th-) percentile from the 1000 bootstraps as the upper (lower) uncertainty.

We will measure how the $\alpha_{\rm CO}$-to-$\Sigma_\star$ relation varies according to the adopted D/M and $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$ in the remainder of this section. In [8](#app:d/m), we also test how the results would change with an internal variations of D/M. Our toy model in [8](#app:d/m) shows that $a$ could be up to $\sim 0.2$ steeper than the constant D/M case.

## Dependence of the power-law index on adopted D/M and $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$

![](DM_evolution.pdf)

To test the robustness of our results for potentially different dust properties, we expand the assumed D/M from the single value (0.55) assumed in the previous section to the possible range of D/M, i.e. $0.1 \leq \text{D/M} \leq 1$. We do not go to even lower D/M values because our methodology relies on the existence of certain amount of dust. We derive $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ and fit the $\alpha_{\rm CO}$-to-$\Sigma_\star$ power-law relation at each assumed D/M. The results are shown in [8](#fig:fit_evolution_DM). We highlight the fit results with $0.4 \leq \text{D/M} \leq 0.7$, which is the D/M value inferred from literature introduced in [2](#sec:calc_aco). Same as in the previous calculations, the uncertainties of parameters $a$ and $b$ in the fitting parameters are estimated from 1000 rounds of bootstrap resampling.

As shown in the top panel of [8](#fig:fit_evolution_DM), we find that the power-law index ($a$) is invariant with assumed D/M throughout the range we examine for both $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ and $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$. The average $a$ in the range of $0.4\leq \mathrm{D/M} \leq 0.7$ is $-0.48^{+0.08}_{-0.09}$ and $-0.22^{+0.08}_{-0.09}$ for $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ and $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$, respectively. The statistical uncertainties in $a$ for both CO transitions are around $\pm0.1$ dex. The result implies that as long as the D/M stays roughly constant within each galaxy, we can recover similar behavior in the $\Sigma_\star$ dependence of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ with a power law

Due to the nature of the definition of $b$ in [\[eq:power law\]](#eq:power law), we expect $b \sim 0$. This is seen in most D/M values we examine as $|b|$ stay below 0.03, shown in the middle panel of [8](#fig:fit_evolution_DM). This indicates that the power law parameterization reasonably fits the observed data regardless of the assumed D/M value. However, the $b$ values for $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ seems biased toward the positive end. This could result from a steeper $\log$$\alpha_{\rm CO}$-to-$\log$$\Sigma_\star$ slope toward higher $\Sigma_\star$, which results in a positive offset in the power law at relatively lower $\Sigma_\star$.

In the bottom panel, we show the $\Delta_\mathrm{rms}$ value of each fit as an indicator of goodness of fit. All fits have $\Delta_\mathrm{rms}$ below 0.2 dex, and the fits around $0.4\leq \mathrm{D/M} \leq 0.7$ have $\ensuremath{\Delta_\mathrm{rms}}\sim0.14$ dex.

![](SST_evolution.pdf)

We further test if the chosen threshold in stellar mass surface density, $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$, will affect the fitting results. We fix $\text{D/M}=0.55$ and fit the power-law relation at $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$ ranges from 30 to 300 $\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}$. Note that the number of galaxies included in the subsample changes in each case due to the threshold in $\Sigma_\star$. The results are shown in [9](#fig:fit_evolution_SST).

In the top panel of [9](#fig:fit_evolution_SST), we notice that the power-law index ($a$) has a larger dynamic range than the case where we alter D/M, but the index stays negative throughout the $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$ range we examine. The power-law index for $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ stays within $\pm0.1$ of the fiducial case, and the indices for $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$ is consistent with the fiducial value at $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}}>60~\ensuremath{\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}}$. There is a weak trend that $|a|$ becomes larger toward larger $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$. The small $b$ values indicate that the power-law function form applies in general. We also show the $\Delta_\mathrm{rms}$ values in the bottom panel. We have $\ensuremath{\Delta_\mathrm{rms}}\leq 0.2$, with a weak trend of smaller $\Delta_\mathrm{rms}$ toward higher $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$.

To summarize, the power-law functional form applies to the normalized $\alpha_{\rm CO}$-to-$\Sigma_\star$ relation within the D/M and $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$ ranges we examine. With a fixed $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$ at 100 $\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}$, we find a invariant power-law index ($a$) throughout $0.1 \leq \mathrm{D/M} < 1.0$. The average $a$ in the range of $0.4\leq \mathrm{D/M} \leq 0.7$ is $-0.48^{+0.08}_{-0.09}$ and $-0.22^{+0.08}_{-0.09}$ for $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(2{\ensuremath{-}}1)}}$ and $\alpha_{\textup{CO}\,\ensuremath{(1{\ensuremath{-}}0)}}$, respectively. With a fixed D/M at 0.55, we find a weak trend of larger $|a|$ toward higher $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$. The power-law index derived with the fiducial setup, i.e. $\mathrm{D/M}=0.55$ and $\ensuremath{\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}}=100~\ensuremath{\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}}$, is a good representative of conditions with $60 < \ensuremath{\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}}\leq 300~\ensuremath{\rm M_\odot~pc^{-2}}$, with a span $\sim\pm0.09$.

## Galaxy-to-galaxy variations

In this section, we examine the possible variation of the $\alpha_{\rm CO}$-to-$\Sigma_\star$ relation between individual galaxies, mainly how the variation in $\alpha_{\rm CO,gal,T}$(normalization of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ at $\Sigma_{\rm\star,T}$, see [5](#sec:aCO-SigmaMstar)) and $a_\mathrm{gal}$ (power-law index, [\[eq:power law\]](#eq:power law)) correlate with galaxy-averaged properties. By understanding what sets $a_\mathrm{gal}$ and $\alpha_{\rm CO,gal,T}$, we can build a prescription of $\alpha_{\rm CO}$ considering the $\alpha_{\rm CO}$-to-$\Sigma_\star$ relation and galaxy-to-galaxy variations. The results are visualized in [10](#fig:plidx_norm_21) and [11](#fig:plidx_norm_10).
